prompt: Two custom checkbox widgets, each pairing a decorative icon with label text: ```html ``` Both widgets use aria-hidden somewhere. One is genuinely accessible; one is broken. Identify which is which, explain precisely what a screen reader announces for each, and state the general rule for when aria-hidden on part of a label is fine versus when it breaks the control entirely.

One developer correctly hid only a decorative icon; the other hid the icon's entire container, including the real label text along with it.
For each widget, ask: after stripping out everything aria-hidden removes, what accessible name is left for the input?
explanation:
Widget 1 is correct. aria-hidden="true" is on the <span> icon only — a legitimate, recommended pattern for suppressing purely decorative content from being announced (without it, a screen reader might read "crescent moon emoji, Enable dark mode, checkbox, not checked" — noisy and confusing). The surrounding label text "Enable dark mode" is not a descendant of the aria-hidden span, so it stays in the accessibility tree, and the label is still properly associated via for/id. VoiceOver announces: "Enable dark mode, checkbox, not checked."

Widget 2 is broken. aria-hidden="true" is on the <label> element itself — the ancestor of both the icon span and the text "Enable compact layout." Because aria-hidden removes its target and every descendant, the entire label subtree — icon and text alike — is pulled from the accessibility tree. The checkbox announces only "checkbox, not checked," with no label at all. The developer likely intended to hide just the icon, like Widget 1, but put aria-hidden on the wrong element.

General rule: aria-hidden on decorative content nested *inside* an accessible label is a good pattern. aria-hidden on the label itself — or on any ancestor that also contains the real accessible text — takes the text down with it and breaks the control.

prompt:
You're reviewing a pull request that redesigns a pricing table. The diff only touches CSS — it adds `order: -1` to the "Recommended" plan's card so it visually renders first among three pricing cards, without touching the HTML at all. The PR description says: "Moved Recommended plan to the front visually, LGTM to merge."

Write the code review comment you would leave. It must: (1) state precisely what will break for keyboard users and why, (2) say what you'd personally verify by hand before approving — not just what an automated scanner would report, and (3) give the specific fix, including what should change and what should NOT need to change.
hints: Think about what an automated accessibility scanner would and wouldn't catch here — that's exactly why manual testing matters for this class of bug.
CSS order and DOM/tab order are two completely separate systems — changing one never changes the other.
A strong review comment names the specific user-facing symptom (what a keyboard user experiences), not just "this violates a rule."
explanation:
A strong review comment covers:

1. **What breaks**: `order: -1` is a purely visual CSS property — it changes rendering position but never DOM/tab order, which always follows HTML source order. If the Recommended card is still third in the markup, a keyboard user tabbing through the page reaches the other two plans before reaching Recommended, even though it now visually renders first — completely out of sync with what they're looking at. This passes an automated scanner with zero errors, since there's no ARIA or semantic violation here — the only way to catch it is to physically tab through the rendered page (mouse aside) and confirm the sequence you land on matches the sequence you see.

2. **What I'd verify by hand**: I'd tab through the live preview myself and note exactly which card receives focus first, second, third — not trust that `order: -1` did what its name implies for keyboard users.

3. **The fix**: move the Recommended card's markup to be first in the HTML source, matching its new visual position. Once DOM order matches visual order, the `order: -1` can be removed entirely — don't stack another CSS property on top to patch a problem that only exists because the source order itself is wrong.

hints: Trace both directions separately — Tab forward from the last element, and Shift+Tab backward from the first element — don't assume the code handles them symmetrically.
Look at exactly what the keydown handler checks: does it ever read e.shiftKey anywhere?
A real trap has to intercept the boundary case in both directions, not just one.
Split the lifecycle into two separate moments and check each independently: what happens the instant the modal opens, and what happens the instant it closes.
Is anything in openModal() actually moving focus into the dialog, or does it just make the dialog visible?
document.body isn't focusable by default — think about what calling focus() on it actually accomplishes.
Don't just re-check the Tab-wrap logic — it's already correct here. Look at every interactive-looking element and ask: can I actually reach it and activate it using only a keyboard?
The 'focusable' NodeList only queries for 'button' elements — check whether every clickable-looking element in the markup is actually a <button>.
Check every place closeModal() is wired up — is there a keydown listener for Escape anywhere, or only onclick attributes?
explanation:
Two real problems remain, even though the trap logic and focus restoration are both solid:

1. **The close "×" is unreachable by keyboard.** It's a `<div class="close-x" onclick="closeModal()">`, not a <button> or <a href>. Divs aren't natively focusable or keyboard-operable — no default tabindex, no keydown-triggered click. Worse, `focusable` is built with `querySelectorAll('#delete-modal button')`, which only matches real <button> elements — the close div isn't in that NodeList at all, so it's silently excluded from the tab cycle entirely. A mouse user sees and can click the × fine; a keyboard user can never reach it and has no way to know it exists, because Tab just cycles between Delete and Cancel.

2. **There's no Escape key handling anywhere.** closeModal() is only ever wired to onclick attributes. A correctly-implemented dialog should close on Escape and return focus to the trigger — here, Escape does nothing at all, even though clicking Cancel and the trap wrapping both work.

Fix priority: the unreachable close button first — it's a complete "this functionality doesn't exist for keyboard users" gap (either give the div `tabindex="0"` plus a keydown handler, or, better, make it a real <button> and include it in the `focusable` NodeList so the trap wraps around it too). Escape-to-close is the close second priority — genuinely expected behavior that's simply missing, but Cancel and Delete remain independently reachable via Tab, so it's a smaller gap than a control that's completely unreachable.

Body text renders at 3.1:1 against its background
A form field's <label> points at an id that doesn't exist

hints: A scanner can compare two colour values and check whether an attribute exists. It cannot judge whether a word is the right word.
If answering the question requires knowing what the content means, it isn't automatable.

The line between the first two columns is **meaning**. A scanner can tell you `alt` is missing; it cannot tell you `alt="product image"` is useless, because checking that requires knowing what the image shows. Same with labels: present-and-associated is machine-checkable, *accurate* is not.

The line between the second two is **behaviour**. A skilled manual reviewer can tell you the heading structure is flat and that this will make orientation hard. Only watching real users tells you they give up at step three because of it, and that is the finding that changes a roadmap.

prompt: A client says: "We run axe on every build and it's been clean for six months, so we're accessible." True or false — and justify your answer in a way the client could act on.

config.rubric: A full answer states the verdict and gives a reason a client could act on — not just which way the answer falls.

hints: What proportion of barriers is the tool even attempting to detect?
What would a clean scan on a page that is entirely unusable by keyboard look like?
The client needs a next step, not just a correction.
explanation:
False — and the useful reply is not "scanners only catch 30%", it's a demonstration. A page can pass every automated check while being completely unusable: semantic HTML throughout, perfect contrast, every image labelled, and a checkout flow where focus is never moved into the payment dialog, so a screen reader user never learns it opened.

A clean scan is genuinely worth having. It means the mechanically-detectable class of defects is under control, which is real and not nothing. It says close to nothing about whether the tasks on the site can be completed. The actionable next step is a keyboard-only pass on the three highest-value journeys — a few hours, no tooling budget, and it will produce findings.

prompt: A reviewer who has used NVDA daily for six years and a reviewer who learned it last month audit the same product page. Both are competent and thorough. Which difference in their findings is most likely, and why?

options.text: The experienced reviewer finds more missing-label defects, because they know the criteria better
The experienced reviewer flags things that technically announce correctly but are unusable at real navigation speed
The new reviewer finds more, because they notice things an experienced user has learned to work around
There is no reliable difference — both are following the same checklist

hints: Which of these differences is about the standard, and which is about how people actually move through a page?
Two of these options describe real effects. Only one is the *most likely* difference.
explanation:
The second option. Missing labels are found equally by anyone who checks; that's checklist work. The difference fluency makes is in the middle ground — a heading structure that is technically valid and useless for orientation, a live region that announces but interrupts, a control whose accessible name is correct and unpronounceable. Those are only visible to someone who navigates by headings and landmarks at speed rather than tabbing through linearly.

The third option is not wrong as a phenomenon — experienced users genuinely do normalise barriers they've worked around for years, and that is a real failure mode worth guarding against. But it makes an experienced reviewer *miss* things, not find more, so it doesn't answer the question asked.

The fourth is the assumption this lesson exists to argue against. If findings were checklist output, fluency would be irrelevant and an automated scan would be sufficient.

prompt: Match each reader of your audit to the thing they most need from it. Each reader needs everything eventually — match them to what they need *first*, in the first thirty seconds.

pairs.right: Reproduction steps, environment, and the specific element
The pattern that caused it, not the instance
Which user journey is blocked, and for whom
Conformance level, criterion cited, and the current exposure
Whether the accessibility statement matches reality

hints: Ask what decision each person is about to make. The thing they need first is whatever that decision turns on.
The designer is not going to fix one button — they own the component every button comes from.
explanation:
One audit, five readers, five different first questions. This is why the standard report structure exists: an executive summary that answers the product owner and legal, findings that answer the developer, and a grouping by root cause that answers the designer.

The procurement case is the one people forget, and it's increasingly where accessibility decisions actually get made — before a product is bought, by someone comparing an accessibility statement against an audit. If your report is the evidence in that comparison, its honesty about scope matters more than its length.

prompt:
You have committed to auditing five user journeys in two weeks. On day three you have a crash and lose four working days. You now have four days for work you scoped at nine.

Write the message you send the client. Then say which parts of the audit you would cut and why — being specific about what the cut costs them.
hints: What does the client need to be able to decide? Give them that, not an apology.
Cutting journeys and cutting depth are different trade-offs with different consequences. Which one preserves the audit's honesty?
There is a version of this message that offers a choice rather than announcing one.
explanation:
The strong version does three things: states the new reality in one line without a medical account, offers a specific choice, and names the cost of each option.

Something like: *"I've lost four working days and have four remaining against nine days of scoped work. Two options. (a) I audit three of the five journeys at full depth — you get findings you can act on immediately, and two journeys stay unexamined, which I'd state plainly in the scope section. (b) I cover all five at reduced depth — automated plus keyboard only, no screen reader pass — which will surface fewer and shallower findings across more surface. I recommend (a): a shallow pass across everything tends to produce a report that reads as reassuring, and this product's risk is concentrated in checkout. Happy to go with (b) if breadth matters more for your deadline."*

The reasoning behind that recommendation is the part worth internalising. Reduced-depth-everywhere is the more dangerous deliverable: it produces a document that *looks* like full coverage and quietly certifies journeys nobody properly examined. Fewer journeys, honestly scoped, is the option that keeps the audit true.

What doesn't belong: an explanation of your health, an apology longer than a sentence, or a silent delivery of reduced work at the original scope wording.

prompt: A page's only navigation is a set of `<div>` elements with click handlers, styled as links. Which of these is the *task-level* statement of the barrier?

options.text: The navigation fails 2.1.1 Keyboard and 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value
A keyboard or screen reader user cannot move between sections of the site at all
The divs should be anchor elements

hints: One of these is a citation, one is a fix, one is a consequence.
explanation: The second. The first is the citation and the third is the recommended fix — both belong in the finding, underneath a first line that says what a person can no longer do.

prompt: True or false: a Level A failure is always more severe than a Level AA failure.

config.statement: Level A failures are always more severe than Level AA failures.
config.rubric: A full answer states the verdict and gives a reason a client could act on — not just which way the answer falls.

hints: Conformance level describes how fundamental a criterion is considered, across all content.
Think of a Level A failure on a decorative element versus an AA failure in a checkout.
explanation: False. Conformance level is a property of the criterion, not of the instance. A missing `alt` on a decorative image is a Level A failure that blocks nobody; insufficient contrast on the only error message in a payment form is Level AA and can stop a transaction. Severity comes from impact, frequency and whether a workaround exists — level is an input to that judgement, not a substitute for it.

prompt: Sort each observation by whether it is a *conformance failure*, a *barrier with no clean criterion*, or *both*.

items.text: A decorative divider image has alt="divider" instead of an empty alt
The form clears all entered data after a 15-minute timeout, with no warning
The only way to dismiss a promotional overlay is a 12x12px close button with no accessible name
Eligibility questions are written at a reading level most applicants can't parse under stress
A required field's asterisk is conveyed by red colour alone

hints: Ask two separate questions of each: does a criterion clearly cover it, and does it stop the task?
explanation: The middle column is the one this module exists for. Timeouts that destroy work and content nobody can parse under stress are among the most common reasons real people abandon government and healthcare services, and neither has a criterion you can point at without an argument. They still go in the report.

prompt: Which of these findings could a well-configured automated scanner detect reliably?

options.text: A `<label>` whose `for` attribute references an id that does not exist on the page
A `<label>` correctly associated with an input, whose text describes the wrong field
A form where focus is never moved to the first error after failed validation
A heading structure that is valid but conveys nothing about the page

hints: Which of these can be decided by looking at the markup, without knowing what anything means?
explanation: Only the first. A broken `for`/`id` reference is a pure markup property. The other three need, respectively: understanding what the field is for, observing runtime behaviour, and judging whether text is meaningful. None of those is available to static analysis.

prompt: Put the five steps of turning an observation into a finding into order.

items: Name the task the user was trying to complete
Name the access method affected, and the environment it was observed in
State exactly where the task stops
State what the user is left with — is there another path?
Cite the success criterion, if one applies

hints: The citation is not the first step, and the reason it isn't is the point of the whole procedure.
explanation: Running this backwards — starting from a criterion and hunting for instances — is what produces audits that are technically complete and practically useless. Task first, citation last.

prompt: Match each audit reader to the section of the report they will read first.

pairs.right: The individual finding with reproduction steps
The executive summary
Findings grouped by root cause
The scope statement and its exclusions

hints: Each of these people is about to make a different decision.
explanation: The procurement reviewer is the one most often designed for last and most often the one whose decision carries the most money. They are reading to find out whether an accessibility claim is backed by anything.

prompt:
A client asks: "Our developers already run an accessibility linter in their editor and we have axe in CI. What would a manual audit add that we're not already getting?"

Answer in under 120 words, without being condescending and without dismissing what they've built.
hints: They have genuinely done something valuable. Say so first, and mean it.
One concrete example of a barrier their setup cannot see will do more than any statistic.
explanation:
A strong answer credits the existing work, then makes the boundary concrete rather than statistical: their tooling covers the class of defects decidable from markup, and covers it continuously, which is better than most organisations manage. What it cannot see is anything requiring meaning, layout or runtime behaviour — so a checkout where focus is never moved into the payment dialog will pass every check they run and be unusable with a screen reader. Then offer the cheap next step: a keyboard-only pass on the top journeys, a few hours, no new tooling.

What weakens an answer: leading with a percentage, or implying their CI setup is theatre. It isn't.

prompt: True or false: because you use a screen reader daily, you are qualified to judge whether an interface's cognitive load is acceptable.

config.statement: Daily screen reader use qualifies a reviewer to judge cognitive accessibility.
config.rubric: A full answer states the verdict and gives a reason a client could act on — not just which way the answer falls.

hints: These are different access needs with different evidence behind them.
The answer should be specific about what you *are* qualified to say.
explanation: False, and the useful version of the answer says what you *can* claim. Screen reader fluency gives you real authority on navigation, announcement quality, structure and operability — write those with confidence. Cognitive load is a different access need; you can review it against known guidance and flag concerns, but "is this comprehensible under stress" is settled by testing with the people it's for. Saying so in the scope section is a mark of a serious reviewer, not a limitation to hide.

prompt: A finding draft reads: "Elderly and disabled users may have difficulty with the small font size on this page." Which rewrite best applies the impairment/barrier/disability distinction from this lesson?

options.text: "Elderly and disabled users struggle to read small text."
"Body text renders at 11px with a 2.8:1 contrast ratio, below the 4.5:1 WCAG AA requires — this is unreadable for anyone with reduced visual acuity, regardless of age or diagnosis."
"Users with vision impairments should use their browser's zoom feature."
"Some users find the font size difficult."

hints: The rewrite should name a measurable property of the design, not a category of person.
"Elderly and disabled" is doing the same job "blind users are limited" did in the lesson's spot-flaw example — locating the problem in a group instead of in a number.
explanation: The correct rewrite names the actual design facts — the size, the measured contrast ratio, the standard it falls short of — and states who it affects by mechanism (reduced visual acuity) rather than by demographic category ("elderly"). That version is also the only one a developer can act on directly: there's a number to change and a number to hit.

prompt: Rewrite this sentence from an internal design doc, applying what this lesson calls locating the disability in the barrier rather than the impairment: "We can't fully support colorblind users because our brand palette relies heavily on red and green to indicate status."
hints: What's the actual design property causing the failure? Name it, not the group affected by it.
"Can't fully support" treats the barrier as a fixed cost of doing business. Is that true, or is it a choice made once that could be made differently?
explanation: A strong rewrite names the design fact directly: "Status is conveyed by colour alone (red/green), with no accompanying icon, label or pattern — this fails for anyone with red-green colour vision deficiency (about 1 in 12 men), and for anyone in bright light where the difference washes out." Note what changed: the sentence no longer treats the exclusion as an unavoidable fact about the brand — it names the specific design choice (colour-only encoding) that produces it, which is also, not coincidentally, the thing that's actually fixable without touching the brand palette at all (add an icon or label alongside the colour).

prompt: A team ships one fix — increasing all touch targets to 48px — and describes the release as "our accessibility update." Which of these is the most accurate description of what actually happened?

options.text: The product is now accessible
One access category (motor) received a real improvement; vision, hearing, cognitive and fluctuating-capacity needs are unaffected by this change
The change primarily helps blind users navigate more easily
Touch target size has no real accessibility impact, so this was cosmetic

hints: Which of the categories from this lesson does a bigger touch target actually address?
"Our accessibility update" implies more categories were touched than actually were.
explanation: Bigger touch targets are a genuine, specific improvement for motor access needs (tremor, limited dexterity, imprecise pointing). They do nothing for a screen reader user, someone relying on captions, or someone whose barrier is a 40-field form with no save point. Describing one category's fix as "the accessibility update" is the exact mistake this lesson opens with.

prompt: True or false: when two access needs genuinely conflict in a design decision, the correct response is to treat the decision as arbitrary, since no option satisfies everyone.

config.statement: When two access needs conflict, the design decision between them is arbitrary.
config.rubric: A full answer states the verdict and names the actual tie-break criterion — task-blocking impact versus added friction — not just that a decision has to be made somehow.

hints: One option in a genuine conflict is usually closer to "cannot complete the task at all." That's not arbitrary information.
The lesson's touch-target example had a specific, defensible answer, not a coin flip.
explanation: False. A genuine conflict between two access needs isn't a coin flip — the useful tie-break is which failure mode is closer to blocking the task outright versus adding friction someone can push through. In the lesson's example, forcing a magnification user into horizontal scrolling and lost context is a heavier cost than a slightly smaller (but still AA-compliant) touch target. Treating every trade-off as arbitrary is what lets a team avoid making — and writing down — an actual decision.

prompt: Sort each access need into permanent, temporary, situational or fluctuating.

items.text: Congenital deafness
A perforated eardrum, healing over six weeks
Trying to read a phone screen in bright outdoor light
A relapsing-remitting condition where fine motor control varies day to day
Holding a baby in one arm, needing one-handed operation
A broken dominant wrist in a cast for eight weeks
Chronic migraine with unpredictable visual aura episodes

hints: Ask two questions: does it come from the body or the environment, and does it resolve on a known timeline?
Situational needs vanish the instant the environment changes. Fluctuating ones don't — they're waiting to come back on their own schedule.
explanation: The two axes that do the sorting: body-vs-environment (temporary and permanent and fluctuating all come from the body; situational comes from the environment), and known-vs-unknown resolution (temporary resolves on a knowable timeline; fluctuating doesn't resolve at all, it recurs indefinitely). Migraine and the relapsing condition both sit in fluctuating precisely because nobody — including the person living with them — can schedule the next bad day.

prompt: A hospital appointment-booking portal requires a caller to complete booking, insurance verification and consent-form review in a single continuous session; there is no save-and-resume anywhere in the flow. Using this lesson's four-step procedure (name the need, state the failure, state what's lost, specify the minimal fix), write the finding.
hints: Which access category does "must be completed in one continuous session" fail specifically?
What's lost isn't just time — for a form involving insurance and consent details, re-entry has its own cost.
The minimal fix should not require redesigning the flow, just letting its state survive an interruption.
explanation: A strong finding: **Access need** — fluctuating capacity, and secondarily anyone interrupted by a phone call, a work obligation, or fatigue mid-session. **Failure** — the flow has no save point across booking, insurance verification and consent review; closing the tab or losing the session discards everything entered. **What's lost** — not just time, but sensitive insurance and medical information re-entered from memory, which is itself a real cost, and for someone with unpredictable capacity, a task that may not get finished at all if the bad moment arrives mid-flow. **Minimal fix** — persist entered data against the patient's account (or a session token emailed to them) at each of the three stages, with a resume link, requiring no redesign of the booking flow itself, just state that survives closing the tab.

prompt: A form has no missing alt text, no keyboard trap, no contrast failure — a clean automated scan — and still has high abandonment because errors only surface after the final submit, with no progress indicator anywhere. Which category of access need does this primarily fail?

options.text: Motor — the form is hard to operate with a pointing device
Cognitive — the design exceeds what a meaningful share of users can hold in working memory with no feedback
Hearing — the form provides no audio alternative
None — a clean scan means there's no accessibility issue here

hints: Nothing about pointing devices or audio is involved in this scenario.
The scan being clean is the point of the lesson, not evidence there's no barrier.
explanation: This is a cognitive access need — specifically, working memory and lack of feedback — and it's exactly the category most likely to pass a clean automated scan while still producing real abandonment, because none of WCAG's testable criteria capture "can a person hold four unconnected pages of context with no progress cue."

prompt: Match each point in a design process to the barrier-producing assumption most likely to enter there.

pairs.right: Interview participants are recruited without specifying disabled representation, so few or none are included
An unstated default of full vision, hearing, mobility and cognition gets baked into 'what the user would expect'
A contrast ratio or font size chosen for visual polish, inherited by every screen that uses the token
Nobody in the room has the lived experience or the authority to flag what's missing
Accessibility work is cut first because it was never on the path to a demo looking finished

hints: Each row is a different point in the same process — think about what's specific to that stage.
The design-system row is the one where a single wrong number does the most damage, because of how many screens inherit it.
explanation: Five different points, five different failure modes — which is also five different, specific places to intervene, each cheaper than the one after it. Catching an assumption at recruitment or in the design system is far cheaper than catching the barriers it produces after forty screens have shipped.

prompt: "Users with cognitive disabilities can't follow this checkout flow." Which rewrite correctly relocates the problem?

options.text: "Some users may find checkout confusing."
"Checkout has seven steps with no progress indicator and no way to see or correct entries from a previous step — this exceeds the working memory most people can hold across an interrupted task."
"Users with cognitive disabilities should ask someone to help them checkout."

hints: Name the design property (steps, missing indicator, no review) rather than the group.
explanation: The correct rewrite names three specific design facts (step count, no progress indicator, no review-and-edit) and states the mechanism (working memory across an interrupted task) rather than naming a category of user as the source of the problem.

prompt: True or false: if an access need only affects a small percentage of users, it's reasonable to deprioritise it in a report.

config.statement: A barrier affecting a small percentage of users should be deprioritised in a report.
config.rubric: A full answer distinguishes frequency from severity and gives a reason a client could act on.

hints: Severity and frequency are two different axes — a rare barrier can still be a hard blocker for whoever hits it.
explanation: False. Prioritisation should weigh severity (does it block the task entirely) alongside frequency, not frequency alone. A barrier that completely blocks a small group from an essential task — say, a payment flow no switch-access user can complete — deserves high priority regardless of how few people that is, because for each of them it's total, not partial.

prompt: Sort each scenario into the access category it primarily illustrates.

items.text: Recovering from cataract surgery, told not to strain your eyes for two weeks
Trying to read subtitles on a phone propped up across a noisy train carriage
A condition causing joint pain that varies unpredictably in severity day to day
Being born with one hand

hints: Ask whether it resolves on a known timeline, never resolves, comes from the environment, or recurs unpredictably.
explanation: Cataract recovery has a known timeline (temporary). Train-carriage subtitle-reading is entirely environmental (situational). Unpredictable day-to-day joint pain has no fixed schedule (fluctuating). Being born with one hand doesn't change (permanent).

prompt: A design system's default line-height was set at 1.2 "because it looked tight and clean" and is now used across 60 screens. Which point in the design process did this assumption enter at?

options.text: Research recruitment
Design system defaults
Timeline pressure near a deadline

hints: The token is set once and inherited everywhere — which stage does that describe?
explanation: A value set once in a shared token and inherited by every screen using it is a design-system default — the stage where a single number does the most damage precisely because of how widely it propagates before anyone checks it against WCAG's 1.5x line-height guidance for readability.

prompt: Put these five points from cheapest to most expensive to fix a barrier-producing assumption at.

items: Research recruitment — before any design exists
Persona creation — before decisions are justified by reference to it
Design system defaults — before screens inherit the token
Design review — before development starts building from the file
Production, after launch — after every screen has shipped with the defect

hints: Each stage downstream has to undo more work than the one before it.
explanation: The cost compounds at every stage a wrong assumption survives past. A defect caught in production means retrofitting every screen that already shipped with it — the same fix that would have cost nothing at the design-token stage.

prompt: Match each access need category to a concrete example of a product barrier that fails it.

pairs.right: Body text at 2.8:1 contrast against its background
A drag-and-drop reorder control with no keyboard alternative
Instructions that only appear after a validation error, never before
A session that discards all entered data after 15 idle minutes with no warning

hints: Match the mechanism of the barrier to the category it primarily blocks.
explanation: Each barrier maps to the access need whose core requirement it violates most directly — sufficient contrast for vision, an alternative input path for motor, up-front guidance for cognitive load, and state that survives interruption for fluctuating capacity.

prompt: A colleague says: "We already interviewed five users for this feature, so we've covered accessibility." In under 100 words, explain what's missing from that claim without dismissing the research that was done.
hints: Credit the real work first — five user interviews is genuinely more than most teams do.
The question that matters: who was in the room, and which access categories does that group actually represent?
explanation: A strong answer credits the interviews as real, valuable research, then asks the specific question that determines whether they cover accessibility: did the recruitment brief specify disabled participants, and across which categories (vision, hearing, motor, cognitive, fluctuating)? Five interviews with five non-disabled participants tell you a great deal about that group and nothing about barriers outside it — the gap isn't the amount of research, it's who was recruited into it.

prompt: True or false: a persona that doesn't mention disability is neutral on the subject — it simply doesn't take a position.

config.statement: A persona silent on disability is neutral on the subject.
config.rubric: A full answer explains what silence defaults to, not just that the statement is false.

hints: What does a team's mental model fill in when a persona doesn't specify vision, hearing, mobility or cognition?
explanation: False. Silence isn't neutral — it defaults to whatever the team already assumes, which in practice is almost always full-capacity, non-disabled. A persona genuinely neutral on the subject would have to say so explicitly ("vision and hearing not specified — do not assume full capacity"), because an unstated default gets filled in with the designer's own experience every time it's used to justify a decision.

prompt: A finding needs a citation for a form field with no programmatic label. Which is the correctly-scoped citation?

options.text: Guideline 4.1: Compatible
Success Criterion 1.3.1 Info and Relationships, or 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value depending on the specific defect
Principle 4: Robust

hints: Only the success criterion layer is testable and citable.
A missing label could be a structure problem (1.3.1) or an exposure problem (4.1.2) — the exact defect decides which.
explanation: The citable layer is always the success criterion. Which specific one depends on the exact mechanism: if the label exists but isn't programmatically associated, that's 1.3.1 or 4.1.2 depending on the markup; naming the guideline or principle alone leaves a developer with nothing to check against.

prompt: True or false: if an implementation doesn't match any documented WCAG technique, it automatically fails the relevant success criterion.

config.statement: An implementation not matching any documented technique automatically fails the criterion.
config.rubric: A full answer explains what is actually normative (the criterion's text) versus informative (the techniques).

hints: What's the actual pass/fail test — the criterion's wording, or the techniques list?
explanation: False. Techniques are informative examples of ways to meet or fail a criterion, not an exhaustive gate. A novel implementation that genuinely satisfies the criterion's own text conforms, whether or not a matching technique document exists yet.

prompt: A client insists on targeting WCAG 2.2 AAA site-wide, believing it means "maximally accessible." What's the accurate response?

options.text: Agree — AAA is strictly better and should always be the goal
Explain that WCAG itself discourages AAA as a general site-wide policy, since some AAA criteria can't be met for all content types, and recommend AA with targeted AAA items where achievable
Refuse — AAA is not a real conformance level

hints: What does WCAG's own conformance section say about targeting AAA broadly?
explanation: AAA is a real, valid level — the accurate response isn't to refuse it, it's to explain WCAG's own stated position: some AAA criteria genuinely can't be satisfied across all content types, so the W3C itself advises against requiring AAA as a blanket policy. AA plus selectively achievable AAA items is the standard, defensible recommendation.

prompt: A vendor's accessibility statement says: "This product conforms to WCAG 2.1 AA." No scope, no date, no mention of what was tested. In under 100 words, explain what's missing and why it matters to a buyer.
hints: What does a bare conformance claim, with no scope stated, implicitly claim — the whole product? Is that likely to be true?
What happens to a claim's accuracy after the next release?
explanation: A strong answer names two gaps: no defined scope means the claim implicitly reads as covering the entire product, which is rarely what was actually tested and is close to unverifiable as stated; and no date means there's no way to know whether the claim still holds after subsequent releases. A buyer should ask what was tested, on what pages or flows, by whom, and when — the same information a defensible audit's own scope section would state.

prompt: A button's label text renders at 20px bold, contrast ratio 3.4:1 against its background. Does this pass SC 1.4.3?

options.text: No — it's below 4.5:1
Yes — 20px bold qualifies as large text, so the 3:1 threshold applies, and 3.4:1 clears it
Can't tell without knowing the button's background colour name

hints: Check WCAG's definition of large text (18pt, or 14pt bold) against the size given here.
20px is roughly 15pt — comfortably over the 14pt-bold threshold.
explanation: 20px bold clears WCAG's large-text threshold (14pt bold, roughly 18.5px), so the applicable minimum is 3:1, not 4.5:1. 3.4:1 passes against the correct threshold — applying the default 4.5:1 without checking the size first would have produced a false failure.

prompt: Sort each image by whether SC 1.1.1's decorative exception (empty alt) genuinely applies.

items.text: A thin horizontal line image used purely to visually separate two sections
A chart showing quarterly revenue, with no data table alternative provided elsewhere on the page
A repeating background texture behind the page header
A product photo that is the only place the item's colour and finish are shown
An icon-only "delete" button with no visible text label

hints: Ask: does this image convey information not available anywhere else on the page?
Purely visual formatting and true background texture are the narrow cases the exception covers.
explanation: The exception is narrow: pure visual formatting or genuinely redundant decoration. A divider line and a background texture convey nothing beyond visual styling. A revenue chart, a product photo showing unique detail, and a functional icon-only button all convey information a screen reader user would otherwise miss entirely — each needs a real, specific text alternative.

prompt: Match each WCAG document type to what it actually is.

pairs.right: Normative — the actual testable requirement
Non-normative — explains intent and rationale per criterion
Non-normative — documented examples of ways to meet a criterion
Non-normative — documented patterns known to fail a criterion

hints: Only one of the four rows is the thing a page is actually measured against.
explanation: Success criteria are the requirement. Everything else — Understanding WCAG, sufficient techniques, advisory techniques, and failures — is informative supporting material: genuinely useful for interpretation and implementation, never itself the pass/fail bar.

prompt: A required field is marked only by rendering its label in red text, with no asterisk, no "(required)" text, and no ARIA `required` attribute. Which criterion governs this specifically?

options.text: 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) — check whether the red meets the ratio
1.4.1 Use of Color — colour is the only means of conveying the required status
2.4.7 Focus Visible — the field isn't clearly focused

hints: The defect isn't about how visible or high-contrast the red is. It's about what colour alone is being asked to communicate.
explanation: This is 1.4.1 Use of Color, not 1.4.3 — the red text might have perfectly fine contrast and still fail, because the failure is that colour is the *only* signal for "this field is required." A colourblind user, or anyone who can't distinguish red reliably, gets no other cue at all. 1.4.3 would apply if the concern were the red text's ratio against its background, a separate and unrelated question.

prompt: A modal dialog opens, its heading is announced correctly by the screen reader, but the aria-checked state on a toggle inside it never updates when the toggle is activated — it always announces "not checked," even after a successful toggle. Name the governing criterion and explain why the reflex citation for "custom ARIA control" would be right here, unlike in this lesson's keyboard example.
hints: This time, ask what's actually broken: is it exposure/state, or operability?
Compare this to the keyboard-toggle example — what's different about the mechanism?
explanation: This is genuinely a 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value defect: the control's *state* (checked/unchecked) isn't being kept in sync with what actually happened, which is squarely what 4.1.2 requires — that the state of a UI component be exposed and updated correctly. Unlike the keyboard example from earlier in this lesson (where the ARIA was fine and the missing piece was a keyboard handler entirely outside 4.1.2's scope), here the defect *is* the ARIA state itself failing to update, which is exactly what the reflex citation happens to get right this time. The lesson isn't "never cite 4.1.2 for custom controls" — it's "check the actual mechanism before citing anything, every time, including when the familiar answer turns out to be correct."

prompt: Which layer of WCAG's structure would you never see cited alone in a defensible finding?

options.text: A success criterion number, e.g. 2.4.7
A principle name, e.g. "Operable"
A success criterion with its conformance level, e.g. "2.4.7 (AA)"

hints: Which layer is testable?
explanation: Principles are too abstract to be citable alone — they group dozens of criteria and aren't testable. Success criteria, with or without their level stated, are the citable unit.

prompt: True or false: a Level AAA criterion is always more severe to fail than a Level A criterion.

config.statement: Level AAA failures are always more severe than Level A failures.
config.rubric: A full answer distinguishes conformance level (achievability) from severity (task impact) and gives a concrete example.

hints: Level tracks how broadly achievable a criterion is across all content, not how much a given failure hurts a given user.
explanation: False. Level correlates with achievability across content types, not with per-instance severity. A Level A keyboard trap on the only way to complete checkout is a harder blocker than a Level AAA reading-level miss on a footer paragraph.

prompt: A required-field asterisk is red, with no other visual or textual indicator. Which criterion?

options.text: 1.4.1 Use of Color
1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum)
4.1.2 Name, Role, Value

hints: Is the concern the ratio of the red, or what the red is the only signal for?
explanation: 1.4.1 — colour is the sole means of conveying which fields are required, regardless of how well the red itself contrasts against its background.

prompt: Sort each item into mandatory (a specific AA or A success criterion requires it) or advisory (best practice, no mandatory AA citation).

items.text: Visible focus indicator on every interactive element
Body text line length capped around 80 characters
A programmatic label on every form field
Writing at a lower secondary reading level throughout

hints: Ask whether a specific Level A or AA success criterion names this requirement directly.
explanation: Focus visibility (2.4.7) and programmatic labels (1.3.1/4.1.2) are mandatory AA/A requirements. Line length and reading level sit in AAA territory (1.4.8, 3.1.5) — genuinely good practice, not a mandatory AA bar.

prompt: Put these steps in the order that produces an accurate citation rather than a reflex one.

items: State the observed failure in plain language, no number attached yet
Identify the specific broken mechanism
Find the criterion whose exact wording matches that mechanism
Read the full criterion text, including exceptions
Check whether a second distinct mechanism also needs its own citation

hints: The plain-language description of the failure always comes before any number.
explanation: Starting from a remembered number and hunting for a matching defect is the reflex-citation trap. Naming the mechanism first, in plain language, is what makes the citation that follows actually correct.

prompt: Match each defect mechanism to its governing success criterion.

pairs.left: No keyboard handler at all on a custom control
pairs.right: 2.1.1 Keyboard

pairs.left: Accessible name doesn't match the visible label text
pairs.right: 2.5.3 Label in Name

pairs.left: Colour is the only way required status is shown
pairs.right: 1.4.1 Use of Color

pairs.left: A moving carousel with no pause mechanism
pairs.right: 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide

hints: Match by mechanism, not by what kind of element is involved.
explanation: Each row pairs a specific broken mechanism with the criterion written for exactly that mechanism — the discipline this lesson is built around.

prompt: A colleague cites "WCAG 2.1" as a blanket justification for rejecting a design in review, with no specific criterion named. In under 80 words, explain what's missing from that objection and how to make it actionable.
hints: What can the designer actually do with "fails WCAG" as written?
explanation: "Fails WCAG 2.1" names no testable layer at all — it's one level more vague than even citing a bare principle. An actionable version names the specific success criterion, the specific element, and the specific mechanism: e.g. "the icon-only save button has no accessible name — fails 4.1.2 — add an aria-label." That's something a designer can fix in the file open in front of them.

prompt: True or false: WCAG's technique documents (sufficient, advisory, failure) are exhaustive — anything not listed is automatically non-compliant.

config.rubric: A full answer states what is actually normative and gives an example of a novel approach that could still conform.

hints: Only the success criteria are normative — what does that make the techniques documents?
explanation: False. Techniques are informative, non-exhaustive examples. A genuinely novel implementation — a new interaction pattern, a new ARIA usage — can satisfy a criterion's actual text without appearing in any technique document, because the requirement is the criterion's wording, not the list of documented ways to meet it.

prompt: A public university's procurement office asks a software vendor for an accessibility audit before finalising a purchase. What's the most likely trigger?

options.text: Litigation naming this specific vendor
A procurement requirement — the university needs a conformance claim before it can sign
A regulatory deadline specific to this one purchase

hints: Who's asking, and at what point in the relationship?
explanation: This is a textbook procurement trigger: a buyer needing due diligence before signing, not litigation or a deadline. Public-sector buyers routinely require this before purchase, tying back to Section 508 or the Web Accessibility Directive depending on jurisdiction.

prompt: True or false: knowing an audit is litigation-driven means you should soften or omit findings that might strengthen the plaintiff's case.

config.statement: A litigation-driven audit should soften findings to avoid strengthening the other side's case.
config.rubric: A full answer distinguishes scope/priority from honesty about findings.

hints: What does the trigger change — where you look, or what you're honest about once you've looked?
explanation: False. The trigger shapes where hours go and what gets prioritised; it never changes what gets reported. Softening findings to serve a party's litigation position isn't a scoping decision — it's the audit stopping being an audit.

prompt: Which of these is an EN 301 549 requirement that has no WCAG equivalent at all?

options.text: Sufficient colour contrast on body text
The reach distance and mounting height of a self-service kiosk's controls
Programmatic labels on form fields

hints: WCAG governs rendered content in a browser. What does EN 301 549 govern beyond that?
explanation: Physical hardware ergonomics — reach, height, control placement — is squarely EN 301 549's non-web ICT scope, with no WCAG equivalent, since WCAG only addresses content, not the physical device it's shown on.

prompt: Sort each organisation by which EU framework most directly applies.

items.text: A municipal government's online permit-application portal
An airline's ticket-booking website
A private, unfunded local art gallery's informational website with no transactions
A public university's learning management system

hints: Ask: public-sector body, named private-sector category, or neither?
explanation: Government and publicly funded institutions fall under the Web Accessibility Directive. Transport ticketing is a named Accessibility Act category. A purely informational private site with no transactions and no public funding sits in the genuinely uncertain territory both directives leave outside their named scope.

prompt: What did the 2024 DOJ rule specifically establish?

options.text: An explicit WCAG 2.1 AA requirement for state and local government websites and apps, under ADA Title II, with phased deadlines
The same explicit requirement for private businesses under Title III
A new federal accessibility statute replacing the ADA entirely

hints: Which Title does this rule specifically address?
explanation: The 2024 rule is Title II-specific: state and local government, WCAG 2.1 AA, phased by population size. It did not extend the same explicit requirement to Title III private businesses, which remains governed by case law rather than a formal rule.

prompt: Match each organisation type to the US framework that most directly governs it.

pairs.right: ADA Title II

pairs.left: A private e-commerce retailer with no government ties
pairs.right: ADA Title III (case law)

pairs.left: A private company selling software to a federal agency
pairs.right: Section 508 (procurement)

pairs.left: A private university receiving federal research funding
pairs.right: Section 504

hints: Ask what kind of organisation it is and what its relationship to government is.
explanation: Four different relationships to government produce four different governing frameworks — the same organisation can even sit in more than one category depending on which relationship is active for a given product or sale.

prompt: Rewrite this accessibility statement sentence so it's honest and specific: "Our app is accessible to everyone, including users with disabilities."
hints: What are the actual, checkable facts this organisation could state instead?
A genuine statement names a standard, a status, and a date.
explanation: A defensible rewrite names a standard and status honestly, e.g.: "This app partially conforms to WCAG 2.1 Level AA. Known issues: the calendar widget is not fully keyboard-operable, and some archived PDF documents lack proper structure. Report a barrier at [contact]. Last reviewed: [date]." The rewrite trades an unfalsifiable absolute claim for specific, checkable facts — exactly the trade this lesson's spot-flaw example made in the opposite, wrong direction.

prompt: True or false: a disproportionate burden claim is defensible as long as the underlying cost of remediation is genuinely high.

config.statement: A disproportionate burden claim is defensible whenever remediation cost is genuinely high.
config.rubric: A full answer names what a defensible claim needs beyond cost alone.

hints: Cost alone, with nothing else shown, is what the lesson's example got wrong.
explanation: False. Cost is one input, not the whole justification. A defensible claim documents cost against actual resources, weighs it against user benefit and usage data, and shows alternatives were considered — a high cost asserted with no supporting reasoning is indistinguishable from an excuse, regardless of whether it happens to be true.

prompt: A VPAT claims "Supports" for a criterion. Direct testing finds a real gap. What does this most likely indicate?

options.text: The entire VPAT is fraudulent and should be dismissed
A specific, checkable discrepancy that should be raised with the vendor directly, whatever the cause turns out to be
Nothing — VPATs aren't meant to be tested against the real product

hints: What's the proportionate response to one gap in an otherwise unverified document?
explanation: One discrepancy is a specific, actionable finding, not proof of wholesale fraud — most VPAT inaccuracies come from unverified sales claims rather than deliberate deception. Naming the specific gap and asking the vendor to address it is the proportionate response.

prompt: You have two days, not three, to spot-check a VPAT before a contract deadline, with sandbox access only. Write the one paragraph you'd send procurement up front, before starting any testing, to set honest expectations.
hints: What does procurement need to know before they see any findings — about scope, method, and what won't be covered?
The goal is to prevent your eventual report from being read as more complete than it is.
explanation: A strong paragraph states the constraint plainly, names the method (a risk-weighted sample of the highest-stakes criteria and flows, not a full audit), and states explicitly what won't be covered given the time available — so that whatever gets reported two days later is read as what it actually is: a scoped spot-check, not a conformance verdict. Sending this before testing starts, not after, is what keeps the eventual findings from being over-trusted.

prompt: A state government website has almost no accessibility work done and a compliance deadline is six months away. Which framework is most directly relevant?

options.text: ADA Title II, with the 2024 rule's WCAG 2.1 AA requirement and phased deadlines
Section 508 procurement rules
The European Accessibility Act

hints: State government — which US title covers that?
explanation: State government websites fall under ADA Title II, now with an explicit WCAG 2.1 AA requirement and phased deadlines from the 2024 DOJ rule.

prompt: True or false: because ADA Title III has no explicit federal web-accessibility regulation, private businesses face no real legal risk from an inaccessible website.

config.statement: Private businesses face no real legal risk under Title III due to the lack of an explicit regulation.
config.rubric: A full answer distinguishes regulatory clarity from actual litigation risk.

hints: What has case law done in the absence of a formal rule?
explanation: False. The absence of a formal rule doesn't mean absence of risk — a substantial, consistent body of case law has found online businesses covered under Title III, with WCAG AA as the practical benchmark courts point to.

prompt: A statement says "partially conforms to WCAG 2.1 AA; known issue: PDF forms lack labels; last reviewed March 2026." How does this compare to "fully accessible"?

options.text: It's weaker, since it admits a flaw
It's stronger, because it's specific, dated, and checkable — exactly what a genuine statement should be
They're equivalent in practice

hints: Which one could a procurement reviewer actually verify?
explanation: Specific and checkable beats absolute and vague, every time — a named gap and a recent date make the claim verifiable, which is what makes it credible rather than weak.

prompt: Sort each item into what a defensible disproportionate-burden claim requires versus what alone is not enough.

items.text: A cost estimate weighed against the organisation's actual resources
A one-sentence assertion that something is "not feasible"
Usage data showing how many people are affected
Alternatives considered, like remediation on request

hints: A defensible claim shows its work; an excuse states a conclusion.
explanation: Cost against resources, usage data, and alternatives considered are the components of a documented, defensible claim. An unsupported assertion is indistinguishable from an excuse, whatever the underlying facts happen to be.

prompt: A VPAT is best described as:

options.text: An independently verified certification
A self-reported conformance claim, useful but not evidence on its own
A legally binding contract term automatically

hints: Who fills it out, and who checks it?
explanation: Self-reported, with no independent verification built into the process — genuinely useful as a starting point, and worth testing against the real product before relying on it.

prompt: Put these steps in order for validating a VPAT before a purchase decision.

items: Identify the highest-stakes claims — the ones that matter most if false
Test those claims directly against the real product
Note the specific method and result for each
Raise any discrepancy as a specific, named finding, not a blanket accusation
State clearly what was and wasn't covered by the check

hints: Prioritisation comes before testing; honesty about scope comes at the end, not as an afterthought.
explanation: Starting with the highest-stakes claims makes limited time count for the most. Ending with a clear scope statement is what keeps a partial check from being read as a full audit.

prompt: A colleague says: "We're a small private business with no government contracts, so none of this applies to us." In under 90 words, give the accurate response.
hints: Which framework is most relevant to a small private business with no government ties — and is it settled or genuinely uncertain?
explanation: A strong answer names ADA Title III specifically: no explicit federal regulation names their situation, but a substantial, consistent body of case law has found similarly-sized online businesses covered, with real litigation risk regardless of the regulatory gap. "None of this applies" overstates the certainty in the business's favour — the honest answer is "genuinely uncertain at the regulatory level, and genuinely risky in practice," not "exempt."

prompt: A client says their budget for a paid accessibility monitoring platform was just cut. What's the accurate response about what this means for their testing capability?

options.text: Automated testing is now impossible for them

axe-core, Lighthouse, WAVE's free tier and the browser's own inspector remain fully available at no cost — they lose site-wide crawling and monitoring dashboards, not the underlying testing capability
They should switch entirely to manual review, since no free automated option is credible

hints: What specifically does a paid tier add on top of the free tools?
explanation: Every core tool in this lesson has a genuinely free, fully functional path. Paid tiers add convenience at scale (crawling, dashboards, monitoring) — losing the budget for those doesn't remove the ability to run real, rigorous automated checks.

prompt: An element has both aria-labelledby pointing at a visible heading and an aria-label attribute with different text. Which supplies the computed accessible name?

options.text: aria-label, since it's more specific
aria-labelledby, since it sits higher in the precedence order
Both are combined into one string

hints: Check the precedence order this lesson's worked example walked through — which comes first?
explanation: aria-labelledby has the highest precedence in the accessible name computation, above aria-label. When both are present, aria-labelledby wins and aria-label is ignored entirely for naming purposes.

prompt: Sort each success criterion's check by whether it's fully automatable, partially automatable (a scanner can flag a candidate for review), or not automatable at all.

items.text: Whether a contrast ratio between two known colour values meets 4.5:1
Whether a heading exists for a content section
Whether that heading accurately describes the content that follows
Whether two elements on a page share the same id attribute
Whether tab order matches visual reading order

hints: Ask: is this a closed computation on values already in the markup, or does it require understanding meaning?
explanation: Contrast ratios and duplicate IDs are closed computations. Heading existence is checkable, but whether it's a good, accurate heading requires judgement. Tab order versus reading order requires comparing rendered visual layout to logical sequence — a comparison of meaning, not markup.

prompt: True or false: if axe-core finds 14 violations and Lighthouse scores the same page 96/100, one of the two tools has a bug.

config.statement: A sharp disagreement between two scanner results on the same page indicates a tool bug.
config.rubric: A full answer explains the actual mechanism — different rule subsets and presentation formats — rather than assuming malfunction.

hints: What does Lighthouse's accessibility category actually run, compared to axe's full ruleset?
explanation: False. Lighthouse runs a curated subset of axe's rules and converts the result to a single weighted score; axe's full report lists raw violations. Both tools can be working correctly and still disagree, because they were never checking identically the same thing in the same way.

prompt: A scan flags "missing form label" on a field that actually has a correctly associated <label for>, sitting inside a collapsed accordion the scanner's crawler never expanded. How should this be classified?

options.text: A false positive — dismiss it

A real defect the scan under-reported rather than over-reported — the label genuinely exists, but this reveals the scanner didn't interact with the page enough to test it, which is worth noting as a coverage gap, not dismissing
Irrelevant, since the field is inside an accordion

hints: Does the label actually exist and work correctly, once the accordion is expanded?
explanation: The field's label is genuinely fine once you check it directly — this isn't a false positive to simply dismiss, it's evidence that the scan's coverage was incomplete because it never interacted with the collapsed accordion. Worth flagging as a scan-coverage note, distinct from either a confirmed defect or a true false positive.

prompt: A developer, facing a deadline, wraps a low-contrast footer text block in aria-hidden="true" to stop a scanner from flagging it, rather than fixing the contrast. Explain, in under 100 words, why this is worse than leaving the violation flagged.
hints: What happens to a screen reader user's access to that content once aria-hidden is applied?
Compare what a sighted user experiences to what a screen reader user experiences after this change.
explanation: Before the change, a sighted user with low vision struggled to read low-contrast text, and a screen reader user could still access the content fully. After the "fix," the sighted user's problem is completely unchanged, and a screen reader user has lost access to that content entirely — the scan goes green while the total accessibility of the page has gotten strictly worse for one group and stayed the same for another. Gaming the rule this way is worse than the original, honestly-flagged violation.

prompt: Six identical, correctly-labelled "Add to cart" buttons sit next to six different products on a page. A scan finds zero violations. What's the accurate description of this situation?

options.text: The page is fully accessible — every automatable criterion passes
The page passes every automatable check while remaining genuinely hard to use for a screen reader user, because uniqueness-in-context isn't something any single-element rule checks
This can't be a real problem if the scan found nothing

hints: What does 'fully accessible' claim, versus what a clean scan actually proves?
explanation: A clean scan proves the automatable, per-element criteria are satisfied — it says nothing about whether six identical control names next to six different products can actually be told apart, which is a relationship between elements, not a property of any one of them.

prompt: A returning client asks to scope this year's audit down to "just an automated re-check," citing four months of clean CI results. Write the two or three sentences you'd say to respond honestly without simply refusing the request.
hints: Credit what the clean CI record genuinely shows before naming what it doesn't.
Propose something concrete — not just "we need the full manual pass," but where specifically manual depth should stay.
explanation: A strong response credits the real evidence (four months with no new automatable regressions is genuinely good, and worth less audit time spent re-checking that specific class), names concretely what it doesn't cover (task completion, control uniqueness, cognitive load — none of which the CI gate has ever measured), and proposes a specific alternative scope: full manual depth on the highest-traffic journeys, lighter-touch review elsewhere. This turns a potential refusal into a defensible, costed answer to a reasonable question.

prompt: True or false: requiring a perfect Lighthouse accessibility score of 100 to merge is a stronger CI gate than blocking on any new axe-core violation.

config.statement: A perfect Lighthouse score requirement is a stronger CI gate than blocking on new axe-core violations.
config.rubric: A full answer explains why a composite score is a weaker, more gameable gate than a rule-by-rule check.

hints: What happens to individual real defects underneath a single composite score?
explanation: False. A composite score can stay at 100 while specific real defects shift underneath it if the scoring weights don't happen to catch them, and a fixed target invites gaming the score rather than fixing barriers. A rule-by-rule, deterministic check with no ambiguity about pass/fail is the sounder gate.

prompt: A team's CI accessibility gate has been green for six months. Which conclusion is actually supported by that record?

options.text: The product is fully usable by disabled users
No new markup-level regressions covered by the ruleset have reached production in that window
A manual audit is now redundant

hints: Which claim is scoped to exactly what the gate actually checks?
explanation: Only the second claim is scoped to what the gate measures. The other two silently upgrade "no new automatable defects" into a much larger claim the gate never had the power to support.

prompt: A scan flags a "duplicate ID" on two elements that genuinely share id="footer-link" in production markup. Real finding or false positive?

options.text: Real finding — duplicate IDs are a closed, verifiable computation
False positive — IDs don't need to be unique
Can't tell without a screen reader

hints: Is this the kind of check a scanner can verify with certainty?
explanation: Duplicate ID detection is a closed, deterministic computation on the markup — genuinely one of the most reliable classes of automated finding.

prompt: Sort each fix by whether it addresses the actual barrier or only satisfies the automated rule's literal check.

items.text: Writing a specific alt description for a product photo
Setting alt="decorative" on a chart that conveys real data
Genuinely raising a button's text contrast to meet 4.5:1
Adding aria-hidden to low-contrast text instead of fixing its contrast

hints: Ask: does the user's actual experience improve, or does the tool just stop checking?
explanation: The tell is always the same: a genuine fix changes what a real user experiences. A rule-gaming fix changes only what the tool measures.

prompt: Roughly what share of WCAG's Level A and AA criteria are fully, reliably automatable?

options.text: Roughly a fifth to a third
Nearly all of them
Essentially none of them

hints: This is a structural ceiling, not a temporary tooling limitation.
explanation: Estimates cluster in the 20-35% range — a real, useful minority, bounded by which criteria are closed computations versus which require understanding meaning.

prompt: True or false: a page that passes every automated check is guaranteed to be fully usable.

config.statement: Passing every automated check guarantees full usability.
config.rubric: A full answer gives a concrete example of something automatable checks can't catch.

hints: Think of the six identical 'Add to cart' buttons.
explanation: False. Six identically-named buttons next to six different products can pass every automatable check and still be unusable for distinguishing which is which — a relationship no single-element rule verifies.

prompt: Which is the soundest thing to gate a CI merge on?

options.text: Zero new axe-core violations, rule by rule
A perfect composite Lighthouse score
A full manual screen-reader pass on every PR

hints: Deterministic and scoped to what automation reliably checks beats a composite score or a bottleneck-slow manual step.
explanation: A rule-by-rule automated check is fast, deterministic, and scoped honestly. A composite score is gameable; a full manual pass per PR would bottleneck every merge.

prompt: Match each tool to what it's actually best for.

pairs.right: Fast, scriptable checks embedded in test suites and CI
A quick built-in signal, already available in Chrome DevTools
Visual overlay, good for explaining findings to a non-technical client
Reading the actual computed name, role and value directly

hints: Match by the specific moment each tool fits, not by which is 'best' overall.
explanation: Each of the four genuinely does a different job — the right question is never 'which tool is best' but 'which moment is this.'

prompt: In under 80 words, explain to a junior developer why a contrast violation flagged on text over a background photo shouldn't be reported without verification, while a duplicate-ID violation usually can be.
hints: What's different about how each check is computed?
explanation: A strong answer names the mechanism: duplicate-ID detection is a closed computation on markup the scanner has complete, reliable access to. Contrast-over-an-image requires the tool to approximate what colour sits behind the text, which is a measurement it can get wrong — the underlying image data isn't something the algorithm reliably samples the same way a human eye or a proper pixel-sampling check would.

prompt: True or false: a six-month clean CI accessibility gate means a manual audit is now redundant.

config.statement: A long clean CI track record makes a manual audit redundant.
config.rubric: A full answer names something a manual audit checks that CI never has.

hints: What has the CI gate never once measured, clean record or not?
explanation: False. The gate has never measured task completion, control uniqueness, or cognitive load — a clean record is real, valuable evidence about the automatable third, and no evidence at all about the rest.
